example: Given a requirement `foo.a.bar` and a named example `foo.a.b.bar`, `foo.*.bar` matches both, in that order. A requirements input stores both full names and their complete raw fenced declarations. Adding another matching definition invalidates the existing input. {cite}`requirements.references.definition_globs` {cite}`requirements.ci.requirements_inputs`
rationale:
The example is only partly covered by its tests.

The only `{test}` reference to `requirements.references.definition_glob_cases` is `src/definition_glob.rs`, `mod[tests]/fn[wildcard_crosses_dot_segments_and_matches_the_whole_name]` (lines 42–54). It is also tagged for `definition_globs`.

**What it covers.** It checks the glob matcher on plain strings:
- `foo.*.bar` is valid.
- `foo.*.bar` matches `foo.x.bar` and `foo.x.y.bar`, so `*` crosses dots.
- The match is anchored to the whole name.
- An empty glob and `foo[bar]` are invalid.

This does support the first clause of the example, that `foo.*.bar` matches both `foo.a.bar` and `foo.a.b.bar`.

**What it does not cover.**
- It never builds a requirement `foo.a.bar` and a named example `foo.a.b.bar`. It does not check that both are selected from a set of definitions, or that they come back in sorted full-name order.
- It never builds a requirements evidence input. Nothing checks that such an input stores both full names in `matches` and their complete raw fenced declarations in `text`.
- It never adds a third matching definition to see the existing input become invalid.

The `requirements.ci.requirements_inputs` implementation in `src/evidence.rs` (`validate_input`, `validate_resolved_input`) and `src/inputs.rs` (`resolve`) has tests, such as `requirements_inputs_omit_option_lines`. None of them is tagged as a test of this example, and I did not confirm that they exercise the glob scenario.

Because the supplied test covers only the matcher part of the scenario, and not the ordering, stored-declaration or invalidation outcomes, the example is not adequately covered. No FIXME or acknowledged-gap comment records this.

text: Given a requirement `foo.a.bar` and a named example `foo.a.b.bar`, `foo.*.bar` matches both, in that order. A requirements input stores both full names and their complete raw fenced declarations. Adding another matching definition invalidates the existing input. {cite}`requirements.references.definition_globs` {cite}`requirements.ci.requirements_inputs`

A definition glob MUST match a complete full name. `*` MUST match zero or more characters, including dots; all other valid name characters MUST match literally. An empty glob MUST be invalid. Every definition selection MUST use this matching rule, including requirements evidence inputs, CLI definition filters, and the authoring `references` tool, and MUST match against both requirements and named examples.

For a requirements input, `requirements` MUST be a {term}`requirements.references.definition_selection`, and Habeas MUST match it against all defined requirements and named examples. It MUST recompute the matches during validation, sort their full names, and compare them with `matches`. It MUST take each match's complete raw fenced declaration, including its opening and closing lines, concatenate those declarations in full-name order with one blank line between them, and compare the resulting raw lines with `text`. It MUST retain every match's current source file and inclusive line range for display and reference coverage. A selection matching no definitions MUST be invalid. Adding, removing, renaming, or changing a matched definition MUST invalidate the stored input; moving an unchanged declaration within the book MUST NOT. Errors MUST identify the selection and affected definitions when available.
A full requirement or example name, or a definition glob, identifying the
requirements and named examples it matches under
